draft.title: Evaluative language
card: Evaluative language is made of words that judge something or show a feeling about it. Gripping, clumsy, moving and dull are all examples.
Some evaluative words are positive, such as gripping and moving. Others are negative, such as clumsy and dull.
A judgement is only an opinion until it is backed up. A fair judgement points to details from the text, such as what happens, what a character does or how the writing sounds.
Compare two sentences. 'The story is gripping' is a bare opinion. 'The story is gripping because the hero is trapped and the clock keeps ticking' gives a reason from the text.
draft.remember: Evaluative words give a judgement. Details from the text make it fair.

a.q: Which sentence uses evaluative language to judge a film?
opts: The film's final scene was deeply moving
The film was released in the middle of May
The film is about two sisters on a farm
The film runs for about an hour and a half
a.why: Moving shows a feeling about the film and judges it. The other sentences only state facts about the film that anyone could check, so they do not judge it.
a.clue: Look for the word that shows a feeling or an opinion.

b.q: Ravi reviews a novel. Which sentence gives a fair judgement backed up with a detail from the text?
opts: The plot drags, as the hero spends ten chapters packing
The plot is terrible and nobody should bother reading it
The plot is very boring, and I think most people agree
The plot is awful, which is why I gave the book one star
b.why: The first option judges the plot and supports it with a detail about what happens in the book. The others give strong opinions, but none points to anything in the text, so they are not backed up.
b.clue: Which option tells you something that happens in the book?

a.best: The film's final scene was deeply moving

b.best: The plot drags, as the hero spends ten chapters packing

problems.detail: Why (b) says 'The first option judges the plot and supports it with a detail', but the options are shuffled. The first option shown is 'The plot is awful, which is why I gave the book one star', which is not backed by a text detail. The why should name the answer by its content ('The plot drags, as the hero spends ten chapters packing'), not by its position.
